title: Counting Receptors by What They Hold

scenes.tts: Langley argued in 1905 that nicotine and curare act on a receptive substance in the muscle cell itself. Nobody could isolate or count it. Until binding was measured, a receptor could only be inferred from a response, such as a contraction in an organ bath. And a response is not the same as occupancy. So how many sites does a tissue hold, and how tightly does a ligand hold them?
scenes.visual: A muscle strip in an organ bath contracts when a drug is added; beside it a boxed receptor with a question mark that cannot be counted; the drug is moved away from 'response' toward the question 'how many sites, how tight?'

scenes.tts: Take membranes that hold the receptor. Add a ligand made radioactive but still biologically active. Incubate until binding and release are equal. That is equilibrium, where K d is ligand times receptor, over the complex. Tight binders take longer.
scenes.visual: A tube of membranes (blobs with receptor posts) and labelled ligand dots; dots bind and leave; arrows in and out equalise; equation Kd = [L][R]/[LR]; a slow-binder bar takes longer.
scenes.narration: Take membranes that hold the receptor. Add a ligand made radioactive but still biologically active. Incubate until binding and release are equal. That is equilibrium, where Kd is ligand times receptor, over the complex. Tight binders take longer.

scenes.tts: Pull the mixture through a filter that traps the membranes. Wash it several times, so unbound label goes. Count the radioactivity left. That is total binding. Repeat with a large excess of unlabelled ligand, which competes the label off the finite receptor sites. What still counts is nonspecific binding. Total minus nonspecific is specific binding.
scenes.visual: Tube is poured through a filter slab; membranes caught, free label passes; counter reads total; second tube with excess unlabelled ligand fills receptor sites, label stays only on filter background; bars total minus nonspecific = specific.
scenes.narration: Pull the mixture through a filter that traps the membranes. Wash it several times, so unbound label goes. Count the radioactivity left. That is total binding. scenes.tts: In saturation, raise the labelled ligand. Specific binding levels off at the number of sites, B max, and is half maximal at K d. In competition, hold the label fixed and add rising unlabelled compound. Its K i is calculated from the I C 50, the concentration that halves binding, with the Cheng-Prusoff correction.
scenes.visual: Left: saturation curve rising to a Bmax line, Kd marked at half; right: competition curve falling with IC50 at its midpoint and Ki = IC50 / (1 + [L]/Kd of the label).
scenes.narration: In saturation, raise the labelled ligand. Specific binding levels off at the number of sites, Bmax, and is half-maximal at Kd. scenes.tts: An idealised example. Zero point eight zero milligrams of protein bind sixty-six femtomoles in total, and eighteen with a hundredfold excess of unlabelled estradiol. Specific binding is forty-eight, so sixty femtomoles of receptor per milligram. Across concentrations, nonspecific binding usually keeps rising, while specific binding saturates. Ten to ninety percent occupancy takes an eighty-one-fold rise in ligand, so the axis is logarithmic.
scenes.visual: Bars 66, 18, 48 with the per-mg arithmetic; then a plot of total, nonspecific (straight rising) and specific (saturating) against concentration, labelled idealised; a log axis with 10% and 90% marks 81-fold apart.
scenes.narration: An idealised example. 0.80 mg of protein binds 66 fmol in total, and 18 with a 100-fold excess of unlabelled estradiol. Specific binding is 48, so 60 fmol of receptor per mg. Across concentrations, nonspecific binding usually keeps rising, while specific binding saturates. 10% to 90% occupancy takes an 81-fold rise in ligand, so the axis is logarithmic.

scenes.tts: Binding is not response. A tissue can give a full response with most receptors empty. These spare receptors can put the E C 50, the concentration giving half the maximum response, below K d. So measure K d by binding and compare. If receptors take up much of the label, curves steepen, so keep depletion under about ten percent. Too short an incubation distorts curves, so measure the time course.
scenes.visual: Occupancy curve and a response curve to its left; EC50 below Kd; comparison control; then a depleted tube (most label taken up), a steepened curve; then a too-short incubation where bound label has not reached its plateau.
scenes.narration: Binding is not response. A tissue can give a full response with most receptors empty. scenes.tts: Lefkowitz and colleagues made radioactive A C T H in 1970. Adrenal extracts bound it, and unlabelled A C T H and five derivatives inhibited binding in proportion to their biological activity. In 1973 Pert and Snyder used tritiated naloxone on rat brain. Binding was saturable, with a K d of twenty nanomolar and a density of thirty picomoles per gram. Fifteen opiates and antagonists competed for the same sites.
scenes.visual: Two finding cards: 1970 ACTH labelled, adrenal extract, derivative potencies vs displacement; 1973 naloxone on brain, saturation curve Kd 20 nM, 30 pmol/g, 15 competitors.

scenes.tts: A binding site for a plant drug strengthened the case that the brain makes its own opioids. In 1975 Hughes, Kosterlitz and colleagues identified two pentapeptides, the enkephalins. In 1974 Brown and Goldstein found that normal fibroblasts bound labelled L D L with high affinity, but cells from five homozygous subjects with familial hypercholesterolemia did not. The binding defect may account for the cells' cholesterol overproduction. Binding counts sites and measures grip; a response is not occupancy.
scenes.visual: Cards for 1975 enkephalins (label displaced by brain peptide) and 1974 FH fibroblasts (normal cells bind LDL saturably, FH cells flat); closing rule.
